about: THE SVEAR, THE GÖTAR AND GOTLAND, 780-1070: who rules, who fights, who raids, what the law is, what passes for money and where the church stands, so the game can say it for any year. Research for the game's writers and for the chronicle, written 4 Oct 2026; the game does not load this file yet; a draft to edit freely. Three peoples, not one kingdom: the Svear round the Mälar bay (realm id 'svear', as in ports_793.json), the Götar inland to the south-west (id 'gotar': not in ports_793.json, they have no port on the chart), and the Gotlanders (id 'gutes'). RULES OF THIS FILE: years are Julian. 'from' and 'to' are whole years so the game can look a year up; where they are a guess the note says so, and 'attested' gives the years in which a source of the time really names the person. certainty: sure / likely / uncertain / late (late = written 150 years or more afterwards, by Snorri, the saga king-lists, the law books or the Guta saga: colour, not record). (?) marks a doubt in the sources or a thing not re-checked tonight. 'kind' sorts the rulers: for 'who is king of the Svear this year' read realm 'svear' and kind 'king' (those rows cover 780-1075; from 995 the year of a change belongs to both the old king and the new); co-kings, a claimant, a jarl, the prefect of Birka and the two peoples who have no king are extra rows. In raids 'where' is a port id from ports_793.json, or empty where no port of ours is the place ('place' then says where). 'what_it_did_to_trade' and 'what_it_means_for_a_merchant' are our reading for the game, not quotations. Rimbert was read tonight in C. H. Robinson's translation of 1921 (public domain; the words in single quotes are his). Adam of Bremen is cited by book and chapter in Schmeidler's count (older editions run a chapter or two off) and is never quoted.

abbreviations.Rimbert: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii (about 870), by chapter; translation C. H. Robinson, Anskar, the Apostle of the North (1921), sourcebooks.fordham.edu/basis/anskar.asp
abbreviations.Adam: Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum (about 1075), by book and chapter (Schmeidler 1917); scholia by number
abbreviations.ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, by manuscript and annal year, the true year in square brackets
abbreviations.Wulfstan: Wulfstan's voyage, in the Old English Orosius (about 890)
abbreviations.Hkr: Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla (about 1230); public-domain translation S. Laing 1844. Late; the skalds' verses he quotes are of the time
abbreviations.GS: Guta saga (written about 1220-1285; one manuscript, Holm. B 64, about 1350). Late. Facts only: the translation (Peel 1999) is in copyright
abbreviations.VgL: the older Västgöta law (about 1220) and its king list (about 1240). Late
abbreviations.U, Sö, Ög, Vg, G, Hs, DR: rune stones by Rundata number: Uppland, Södermanland, Östergötland, Västergötland, Gotland, Hälsingland, Denmark

realm_ids.svear: The Svear (Sueones, Sweon): Uppland and the shores of the Mälar bay, then an arm of the sea. Market: birka to about 975, then Sigtuna (no port id yet). Kings' seat and great thing: uppsalir.
realm_ids.gotar: The Götar (Gauts, Beowulf's Geats): Västergötland and Östergötland, inland farmers with their own law and thing. No port on the chart. Under the same king as the Svear from about 995 (?).
realm_ids.gutes: The Gotlanders (Gutar): island farmers who are the Baltic's merchants. No king and no town, only beach harbours such as paviken. They pay the Svear king a yearly tribute and keep their own law.

rulers.name: not recorded
rulers.title: king of the Svear
rulers.how_ended: not recorded
rulers.source: No writer of the time names a Svear king before 829. The saga king-lists (Hervarar saga, 13th century) put Björn Ironside and his sons here: legend, not to be used as fact.
rulers.note: The game can say: the Svear have a king at Uppsalir; nobody in Dorestad knows his name.

rulers.name: Erik
rulers.title: king of the Svear
rulers.how_ended: Died. By 852 the Svear had begun a temple to him and were making offerings to him as to a god.
rulers.source: Rimbert 26: the gods' message offers 'to summon your former King Eric to join us so that he may be one of the gods'. ARF 813: Godfred's sons come home from exile among the Svear.
rulers.note: (?) The years are a guess. Rimbert only says he was dead by 852; Robinson's notes and the saga lists both put an Erik before Björn. Whoever was king about 810-813 sheltered the exiled sons of the Danish king Godfred.

rulers.name: Björn
rulers.title: king of the Svear
rulers.how_ended: not recorded
rulers.source: Rimbert 11, 14 (Robinson prints Biörn; Latin Bern). The sagas' Björn at Haugi may be the same man (?).
rulers.note: He received Anskar at Birka, talked it over with his friends and let him preach. Robinson's notes take the king who was away when the Danes came (between 845 and 851) to be Björn still: the end year 850 is a guess (?).

rulers.name: Herigar (Hergeir)
rulers.title: prefect of Birka and counsellor of the king
rulers.how_ended: Died a Christian, with the priest Ardgar beside him, about 851.
rulers.source: Rimbert 11, 19.
rulers.note: The man a merchant at Birka really deals with. He was baptised in 829-831, built the first church on his own family land, and held the town when the Danes came.

rulers.name: Anund
rulers.title: king of the Svear, then an exile
rulers.how_ended: Driven from his kingdom; an exile among the Danes; came back with 21 Danish ships and 11 of his own, took a ransom from Birka, gave it back and stayed 'for some time' to make his peace. What became of him is not recorded.
rulers.source: Rimbert 19 (Latin Anoundus). The sagas make an Anund Uppsale the brother and co-king of Björn at Haugi (late).
rulers.note: (?) Whether he ruled with Björn or before him is not known; the years are a guess.

rulers.name: Olof
rulers.title: king of the Svear
rulers.how_ended: not recorded
rulers.source: Rimbert 26-28, 30 (Robinson prints Olef and Olaf).
rulers.note: He told Anskar he could not decide alone, put the matter to the lots and to two things, and about 854 led the host against the Curonians. The king who kindly received the priest Rimbert in the 860s is not named (Rimbert 33); the end year is a guess (?).

rulers.name: Erik Anundsson (?)
rulers.title: king of the Svear
rulers.how_ended: Died in his bed when Harald Fairhair had been king ten years (Snorri).
rulers.source: Hkr, Harald Fairhair's saga (?); Hervarar saga's king list. No source of the time.
rulers.note: Said to have held Värmland and Västergötland against Harald of Norway. Wulfstan, about 890, names no king but says Blekinge, Möre, Öland and Gotland belong to the Svear.

rulers.name: Björn Eriksson (?)
rulers.title: king of the Svear
rulers.how_ended: Died of age after fifty years (Snorri).
rulers.source: Hkr, Harald Fairhair's saga (?); Hervarar saga. No source of the time.
rulers.note: A reign of fifty years is a saga's round number. Use the name lightly: a Svea asked in these years might only say 'the king at Uppsalir'.

rulers.name: Ring
rulers.title: king of the Svear
rulers.how_ended: not recorded
rulers.source: Adam I.61: when Archbishop Unni came to Birka the Svear were ruled by Ring with his sons Erik and Emund.
rulers.note: The sons ruled with him. The first and last years are guesses (?).

rulers.name: Emund Eriksson
rulers.title: king of the Svear
rulers.how_ended: not recorded
rulers.source: Adam II.25 (?): Emund son of Erik, an ally of Harald Bluetooth of the Danes and not unfriendly to Christians.
rulers.note: Adam does not say whose son this Erik was. The years are a guess (?).

rulers.name: Erik the Victorious (Erik Segersäll)
rulers.title: king of the Svear
rulers.how_ended: Died about 995, at Uppsalir by Snorri's account; a heathen again after a baptism in Denmark.
rulers.source: Adam II.30, 35, 38 (?); Thorvald Hjaltason's verses; the Hällestad stone (DR 295) and the Sjörup stone (DR 279).
rulers.note: The first Svear king of whom much is known. He beat his nephew Styrbjörn on the Fyris fields about 985, is said by Adam to have held Denmark for a time, and most likely laid out Sigtuna about 980.

rulers.name: Olof Björnsson (?)
rulers.title: king of the Svear, with his brother Erik
rulers.how_ended: Died at a meal, poisoned by the saga's account (?).
rulers.source: Styrbjarnar þáttr; Hervarar saga. No source of the time.
rulers.note: Father of Styrbjörn the Strong in the sagas.

rulers.name: Olof Skötkonung
rulers.title: king of the Svear, and of the Götar (REX SVEVORUM on his pennies)
rulers.seat: Sigtuna (no port id; laid out about 980); from about 1014 mostly in Västergötland (Skara, Husaby) (?)
rulers.how_ended: Died in the winter of 1021-1022 (Snorri's reckoning). From about 1019 the Svear had made him share the kingship with his young son Anund.
rulers.source: Adam II.39, 58; his Sigtuna pennies; Bruno of Querfurt's letter to Henry II, 1008; Hkr, St Olaf's saga (late).
rulers.note: The first king to strike coin and the first to stay Christian. He fought at Svolder in 1000 beside the Danish king. Adam says he wished to pull down the temple at Uppsalir and was made to keep his faith to one province: hence the see at Skara. The byname may mean 'tribute king' (?).

rulers.name: Ragnvald Ulfsson
rulers.title: jarl in Västergötland
rulers.how_ended: Went east with the king's daughter Ingegerd when she married Yaroslav in 1019, and was given aldeigjuborg to hold (Snorri).
rulers.source: Sigvat Thordarson, Austrfararvísur (about 1019), which names a jarl Ragnvald; Hkr, St Olaf's saga (late).
rulers.note: The years are a guess (?).

rulers.name: Anund Jacob
rulers.title: king of the Svear and the Götar
rulers.how_ended: Died about 1050 with no living son; his half-brother followed him.
rulers.source: Adam II.59, 61, 73; III.15; ASC (E) 1025 [1026]; his Sigtuna pennies (ANUND REX).
rulers.note: Christened Jacob; the Svear would not have a king with a foreign name and called him Anund (Adam). The VgL king list calls him Kolbränna, the coal-burner, for burning men's houses as a penalty (late). Co-king with his father from about 1019.

rulers.name: Cnut
rulers.title: king of England, Denmark, the Norwegians and 'part of the Svear'
rulers.seat: Winchester and Roskilde (not ports of ours)
rulers.how_ended: The claim is not heard of again after about 1030 (?).
rulers.source: Cnut's letter of 1027 to the English (kept by John of Worcester and William of Malmesbury); Sigtuna pennies reading CNUT REX SW, which may only be copies of English dies (?).
rulers.note: After the fight at the Holy River in 1026. What 'part of the Svear' meant is argued over: perhaps Blekinge, perhaps men at Sigtuna who took him as lord.

rulers.name: Emund the Old
rulers.title: king of the Svear and the Götar
rulers.how_ended: Died about 1060. His son Anund had died on campaign: the old line of kings ended with him.
rulers.source: Adam III.15-16; IV scholion 123 (?).
rulers.note: Adam, who had Bremen's side of the quarrel, calls him the worst; the VgL king list calls him Slemme, the bad (late). He kept his own bishop, Osmund, and turned Bremen's bishop away at the thing.

rulers.name: Stenkil
rulers.title: king of the Svear and the Götar
rulers.seat: Sigtuna (no port id); a Västergötland man
rulers.how_ended: Died in 1066, about the time Harald of Norway fell in England.
rulers.source: Adam III.15-16, III.53, IV.30.
rulers.note: Emund's stepson or nephew by Adam, his son-in-law by Hervarar saga (late). He helped the bishops, set up the see at Sigtuna, and stopped them burning the temple at Uppsalir.

rulers.name: Erik and Erik
rulers.title: two rival kings of the Svear
rulers.how_ended: Both fell in the war between them, with many of the great men of the Svear.
rulers.source: Adam III.53.
rulers.note: Nothing else is known of either. Later writers guess that one was Christian and one heathen (?).

rulers.name: Halsten Stenkilsson
rulers.title: king of the Svear
rulers.how_ended: Driven out.
rulers.source: Adam III.53 with scholion 84.
rulers.note: Stenkil's son. He comes back as co-king with his brother Inge about 1079, after the game's end.

rulers.name: Anund from Rus (Anund Gårdske)
rulers.title: king of the Svear
rulers.how_ended: Cast out at the thing because he would not sacrifice for the people. Håkan the Red follows (about 1075-1079).
rulers.source: Adam III scholion 84; IV scholion 140 (?).
rulers.note: Sent for from Rus (Gardar). The end year is a guess (?).

rulers.name: no king named: the thing of all Götar and its lawman
rulers.title: the thing and the lawman
rulers.seat: Skara for Västergötland; Linköping (?) for Östergötland (not ports)
rulers.how_ended: From about 995 Olof Skötkonung is king of both peoples; the Götar keep their own law and lawman (?).
rulers.source: No record of the time. The Sparlösa stone (Vg 119, about 800) names an Alrik, son of Erik, and Uppsala; the reading is disputed (?). VgL (late): the Svear take the king and may cast him out; he must then ride round the land and be taken by each thing.
rulers.note: When and how the Götar came under the Svear kings is an old open question. The game should not show a 'king of the Götar'.

rulers.name: no king: the Gutnalthing, the thing of all Gotlanders
rulers.title: the thing; a yearly tribute to the Svear king
rulers.seat: Roma, in the middle of the island (not a port)
rulers.how_ended: Did not end: Gotland keeps its own law and thing through the whole game.
rulers.source: Wulfstan, about 890: Gotland belongs to the Svear. GS (late) for the treaty, the thing and the first churches.
rulers.note: The island has judges and farmers, no lord and no town. The Svear king's men come to the thing once a year for the silver and go home.

rulers.name: Olaf, his sons Gnupa and Gurd, then Sigtrygg Gnupason
rulers.title: kings at Hedeby, come from the Svear
rulers.how_ended: Gnupa was beaten by Henry I of the East Franks in 934, paid tribute and took baptism; Sigtrygg was put out by Hardegon soon after.
rulers.source: Adam I.48, 52 (on the word of King Sven Estridsson); Widukind I.40; the two Sigtrygg stones at Hedeby (DR 2, DR 4), raised by Asfrid, Gnupa's wife; chronicle_793.json: 934-gnupa-tribute.
rulers.note: For a generation the same people hold both ends of the crossing from Hedeby to Birka. The years are a guess; some scholars now doubt that the house came from the Svear (?).

wars.who: The Danes, then King Olof and the Svear, against the Curonians (Cori)
wars.what: The Curonians had long before thrown off the Svear. In about 853 a Danish fleet tried to take them, lost half its men and had its ships plundered of gold, silver and arms. The next year Olof came with a great host, plundered and burnt Seeburg (said to hold 7,000 fighting men), sent the ships away and marched five days inland to Apulia (15,000 men). After eight days of fighting the Svear cast lots, found none of their gods willing, and on the advice of merchants in the host asked Christ. The town then offered the Danish spoil of the year before, half a pound of silver for each man inside, the old tribute and thirty hostages. The king took it, against the young men's wish.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The amber and slave coast across from Gotland pays the Svear again. grobin is burnt and is never the place it was. For a year or two no ship is safe on that shore; after it a Svea or Gotland skipper trades there under the king's peace.
wars.source: Rimbert 30 (Robinson prints Aputra for Apulia: Apuolė in Lithuania; Seeburg is usually taken to be Grobiņa). The years follow from Anskar's second visit in 852 (?). chronicle_793.json: 854-courland-war.

wars.who: King Erik of the Svear against Harald Fairhair of Norway (?)
wars.what: By Snorri's account the Svear king took Värmland and claimed Västergötland to the Göta river; Harald took Värmland back and fought the Götar on both banks of the river for a summer or two.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: If true, the Göta river mouth and the roads from Viken into Götaland were shut in those summers. Use as a rumour, not as a dated event.
wars.source: Hkr, Harald Fairhair's saga (?). No source of the time.

wars.who: A house of kings come from the Svear, holding Hedeby; ended by Henry I of the East Franks and then by Hardegon
wars.what: Adam says Olaf came from the Svear land and took the Danish kingdom by arms; his sons Gnupa and Gurd and his grandson Sigtrygg held it after him. Two rune stones at Hedeby, raised by Gnupa's wife Asfrid for their son King Sigtrygg, show they were real. In 934 Henry I beat Gnupa and made him pay tribute and take baptism.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The road from the North Sea to the Baltic (sliesthorp) and the market at its far end (birka) answer to kin. These are the great years of the eastern silver: a Frisian who reaches Hedeby can ship for Birka with Svear who are at home in both.
wars.source: Adam I.48, 52; Widukind I.40; DR 2, DR 4. The first year is a guess (?).

wars.who: Erik the Victorious against his nephew Styrbjörn, who had Danes with him (and, by the sagas, the Jomsvikings)
wars.what: Styrbjörn came up the Mälar bay with a fleet to take the kingship and was beaten in a fight of several days on the Fyris fields below Uppsalir. Rune stones in Skåne remember men who 'did not flee at Uppsala'.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: A hostile fleet in the Mälar bay in the very years when Birka is dead and Sigtuna new. A summer to stay out of the bay; after it the winner's name and his new town are safe.
wars.source: Thorvald Hjaltason's verses in Styrbjarnar þáttr; Saxo; Knýtlinga saga (all late); DR 295 (Hällestad), DR 279 (Sjörup), Ög 81 (Högby: a man 'fell on the Föri'). The year is 984-986 (?); some historians doubt the battle, and the stones may speak of another fight.

wars.who: Erik the Victorious against Sweyn Forkbeard of the Danes
wars.what: Adam says Erik came against Denmark with a great host, beat Sweyn at sea and held the kingdom while Sweyn lived as an exile, until Erik died. Erik had a pact with Bolesław of the Poles and a wife from his house.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: If Adam is right, for two or three years one king holds Hedeby, the Sound and Sigtuna, and a ship pays one lord from the Eider to the Mälar bay. But Sweyn was raiding England in 994, so the tale may be much too big.
wars.source: Adam II.30, 34-35, 38 (?), on the word of King Sven Estridsson. The years are a guess (?).

wars.who: Olof Skötkonung and Sweyn Forkbeard, with Jarl Eirik of Lade, against Olaf Tryggvason of Norway
wars.what: Olaf Tryggvason was caught at sea in the western Baltic and killed. Norway was shared out; by Snorri the Svear king's share was part of Trøndelag and the coast south of the Göta river mouth (Ranrike), held for him by Jarl Svein.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: For some fifteen years the Svear king has a say at the Göta river mouth and on the Viken coast: the western door of Götaland.
wars.source: Adam II.40; Hkr for the shares (late). chronicle_793.json: 1000-09-09-svolder.

wars.who: Men of Uppland and Södermanland in the fleets of Tosti, Thorkell the Tall and Cnut, against the English
wars.what: Not the king's war: shipmen hired themselves to the Danish leaders and came home with shares of the gelds. Ulf of Borresta took three: Tosti's, Thorkell's and Cnut's.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: English pennies pour into the Mälar lands and Gotland; more of King Æthelred's coin has been dug up there than in England. A man home from England has silver to spend and wants cloth, wine and a good sword; while he is away his farm lacks hands.
wars.source: Rune stones U 344 (Yttergärde), U 241, U 194; the coin hoards. chronicle_793.json: 1007-tribute, 1018-heregeld.

wars.who: Olof Skötkonung against Olaf Haraldsson of Norway
wars.what: Olaf Haraldsson drove out the jarls, took back the lands the Svear king had held since Svolder and killed his tax men. Four years of border raids followed. By Snorri the farmers at the Uppsala thing, with the lawman Thorgny speaking for them, made the king choose peace; it was sworn about 1019 at Kungahälla, and Olaf of Norway married the king's daughter Astrid.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The roads between Viken and Västergötland are shut; Snorri says Olaf of Norway forbade herring and salt to be carried from Viken into Götaland (?). The Svear king loses standing at home and must share the kingship with his son.
wars.source: Sigvat Thordarson, Austrfararvísur (about 1019), the poem of his ride east to Jarl Ragnvald; Hkr, St Olaf's saga, for the thing and the peace (late).

wars.who: Anund Jacob and Olaf Haraldsson of Norway against Cnut
wars.what: While Cnut was in England the two kings harried Skåne and Sjælland. Cnut came with an English and Danish fleet and met them at the Holy River. The English annal says many of Cnut's men were lost and the Svear held the field; the skalds say Cnut won. Either way the allies went home, and the next year Cnut called himself king of part of the Svear.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Fleets in Skåne and the Sound for a summer: no time to pass ahus or the Sound with a cargo. After it Cnut holds the whole road from London to the Baltic, and for a few years his name is on pennies at Sigtuna.
wars.source: ASC (E) 1025 [1026]; Sigvat's and Ottar the Black's verses; Cnut's letter of 1027. The river is most often taken to be the Helge å in Skåne, by ahus; a site in Uppland has been argued (?).

wars.who: Olaf Haraldsson, with men given him by Anund Jacob, against the Norwegian farmers and Cnut's party
wars.what: Olaf came back from Rus through the Svear land; Anund gave him 400 picked men and guides over the mountains. He fell at Stiklestad on 29 July 1030.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Little, at sea. But within a few years Olaf is a saint from Trondheim to Gotland, and 29 July (Olaf's mass) becomes a day for markets and oaths all over the north.

wars.who: Ingvar 'the Far-Travelled' and a fleet from the Mälar lands, in the east
wars.what: A great venture went east through Rus to Serkland, the Saracens' land, 'far after gold' as one stone says. It ended in sickness and defeat; Ingvar died in 1041 by the Icelandic annals. Twenty-six rune stones, nearly all round the Mälar bay, were raised for men who did not come home; none for a man who did.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: A generation of shipmen and their silver gone. It is the last great attempt on the east way to the Saracens: after it the Svear and Gotlanders trade to Novgorod and no further, and their silver comes from Germany and England.
wars.source: The Ingvar stones (Sö 179 Gripsholm and others); Icelandic annals under 1041; Yngvars saga víðförla (late). The first year and the route are guesses (?); a part in the Georgian battle of Sasireti (1042) has been argued (?).

wars.who: Sven Estridsson, with Anund Jacob behind him, against Magnus of Norway and Denmark
wars.what: Sven, who had served Anund twelve years, fought Magnus for Denmark, and after each defeat fled back to the Svear and came again with new men. Magnus died in 1047 and Sven had Denmark.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Skåne, the Sound and the Danish isles are a war ground most summers; a Svear harbour is where a beaten fleet refits. Good years to sell rope, sailcloth and arms at Sigtuna, bad years to cross the Sound.

wars.who: Anund, King Emund's son, against a people across the sea whom Adam calls the land of women
wars.what: The king sent his son over the sea to widen the realm. Adam says the people poisoned the springs, and the king's son and his host died. The place is most likely Kvenland, at the head of the Bothnian sea.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The fur country of the far north stays out of the king's hands. The king has no heir, and four years later the old line ends.
wars.source: Adam III.16; IV scholion 123 (?). The year is a guess (?).

wars.who: Two men named Erik, each claiming the kingship after Stenkil
wars.what: Both kings and many of the great men fell. The bishops meant for Sigtuna and Skara stayed away for fear. Halsten was taken as king and driven out, then Anund from Rus.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: No king's peace in the Mälar bay for a year or more, and no bishop. Sigtuna's plot-holders look after their own; a stranger without a host or a guild-brother should lie at Gotland instead.

raids.place: at sea, about half-way between sliesthorp and birka
raids.what: The merchant convoy carrying Anskar and Witmar to the Svear fought, held for a time and was beaten. The pirates took the ships and everything in them: the emperor's gifts and 'nearly forty books'. The men got ashore and went on by foot and by boat.

raids.who: the exiled king Anund, with 21 Danish ships and 11 of his own
raids.what: The king was away. Herigar the prefect, the merchants and the people fled to a stronghold close by and bought peace for 100 pounds of silver. The Danes said 'each individual merchant in the place had more' and wanted to burn the town; Anund had them cast lots, the lots forbade it, and they sailed off. Anund gave the silver back and stayed to make his peace.
raids.source: Rimbert 19. The year is somewhere between 845 and 851 (?). Robinson's note calls the stronghold Sigtuna, which did not yet exist; the fort on the rock beside Birka fits.

raids.place: a town 'on the borders of the lands belonging to the Slavonians', not named
raids.who: the same Danish fleet, sent there by the lots
raids.what: They fell on a town that was living in peace, took it by arms and went home with much spoil.
raids.source: Rimbert 19. Which town is not known (?); reric was already gone (808).

raids.place: the Curonian coast; which of their five towns is not said
raids.what: The Curonians gathered, beat them, killed half and plundered their ships of gold, silver and arms.
raids.source: Rimbert 30. The year is the one before Olof's war (?).

raids.what: The town was plundered and burnt; the host then left its ships and marched inland to Apulia (see wars).

raids.place: the road to the port of Schleswig
raids.what: The priest Ragenbert, on his way to take ship with merchants bound for Birka, was waylaid and stripped of all he had; he died of it on the feast of the Assumption (15 August).
raids.source: Rimbert 33. The year is between about 858 and 864 (?).

raids.place: the warriors' hall by the fort at Birka
raids.what: The hall of the town's fighting men was stormed and burnt at about the time the town was given up (?). No writer records an attack; the ground does.
raids.source: Archaeology: the 'Garrison' at Birka (Holmquist; Hedenstierna-Jonson) (?). The year is a guess within 965-985. Adam I.60 says the people of Birka, often raided by pirates, had blocked the channel with sunken rocks (written a century after the town died).

raids.who: Jarl Eirik Hakonarson of Lade, an exile with ships from the Svear king
raids.what: He lay off Gotland most of a summer, taking the merchant ships bound for the island, and landed to plunder along the shore.
raids.source: Eyjolf Dadaskald's Bandadrápa, as Snorri quotes it in Hkr, Olaf Tryggvason's saga (?). The year is a guess (?).

raids.what: He besieged and took the town, killed many, broke down and burnt the stronghold, and harried in Rus for some summers after.
raids.source: Bandadrápa in Hkr, Olaf Tryggvason's saga (?). The year is the usual one (?).

raids.place: Soti's skerry in the Svear skerries, then the shores of the Mälar bay
raids.who: Olaf Haraldsson of Norway, a boy of about twelve, with his foster-father's crew
raids.what: His first fight was at a skerry off the Svear coast; then he harried both shores of the bay. By Snorri's tale King Olof chained the sound to trap him and he got out by a channel dug through a neck of land.
raids.source: Sigvat Thordarson's Víkingarvísur (of the time) for the fight; Hkr, St Olaf's saga, for the rest (late). The year is 1007 or 1008 (?).

raids.what: He came in autumn to plunder. The Gotlanders met, sent men to him and offered tribute; he took it and lay the winter on the island. In spring he went on to Ösel.
raids.source: Ottar the Black's Höfuðlausn (of the time), which says the Gotlanders paid him; Hkr, St Olaf's saga (late). The year is 1007 or 1008 (?).

laws.what: At Birka the king hears a stranger's request, talks it over with his friends and, with the consent of all, gives leave: the Christians may stay and preach, and whoever wishes may listen.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A king's word alone opens nothing. Ask through the prefect and expect the answer after the king has met his men. There are Christian captives in the town already: slaves are an ordinary ware here.

laws.what: King Olof's rule in his own words: 'It is our custom that the control of public business of every kind should rest with the whole people and not with the king.' A matter goes first to the chief men and the lots, then to the thing at Birka, then to a second thing in another part of the kingdom.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Three hurdles and weeks of waiting. The best help is an old man of standing who will speak for you at the thing. What the people drove out, the king cannot bring back alone.

laws.what: Leave given by king and things: churches may be built, priests may come, and whoever wishes may be a Christian 'without let or hindrance'. The king grants a plot for a hall of prayer in Birka; the bishop buys a second yard and house for the priest.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A Christian merchant can hear mass at Birka from now until the priests stop coming (after 865). A yard in the town can be bought, or had from the king.

laws.what: A man who has killed may flee to a vi, a holy place, and is safe there while terms are made. Gunnar cut it into the rock at Oklunda in Östergötland: he fled under guilt and sought this vi.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Holy ground is a refuge, heathen as well as Christian, and no one draws a weapon there. A crewman in trouble can run to one.
laws.source: The Oklunda inscription (Ög N288), 9th century (?); the year is a guess.

laws.what: The Forsa ring from Hälsingland, the oldest law text of the north: for not restoring a vi as the people's law requires, one ox and two öre the first time, two oxen and four öre the second, four oxen and eight öre the third; after that the property is forfeit.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Fines are reckoned in oxen and in öre of silver by weight, and double each time. The law is 'the people's', not the king's.
laws.source: The Forsa ring (Hs 7), now dated to the 9th or 10th century; the reading is argued (?). The year is a guess.

laws.what: Gotland's treaty with the Svear king, made by Avair Strabain of Alva: the island pays 60 marks of silver a year, 40 to the king and 20 to the jarl. In return Gotlanders go to every place under the Svear king free of toll and all charges, and the Svear may come to Gotland with no ban on grain or anything else. The king sends men to the Gutnalthing for the silver.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A Gotland skipper pays no toll at Birka or Sigtuna; a Frisian does. Ship as a Gotlander's partner and the goods may go free (?). On Gotland itself there is no king's toll man, only the farmer whose beach it is.
laws.source: GS (late). Put before about 890 because Wulfstan then counts Gotland as the Svear's; the treaty has no date of its own (?). The same text makes Gotland owe seven ships to the king's levy against heathen lands, or 40 marks in coin for each: that rule is later still, after the conversion.

laws.what: Wulfstan's report to King Alfred: sailing east from Hedeby, the Danish lands lie to port as far as Skåne; Bornholm has a king of its own; then Blekinge, Möre, Öland and Gotland, which all belong to the Svear.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: From the east end of Skåne northward the whole coast is in the Svear king's peace. Bornholm answers to nobody else. Skåne and the isles are Danish.

laws.what: Sigtuna is laid out by the king as one long street with narrow plots on both sides, given to his great men, with the king's own yard in the middle.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Birka was an open market island. Here every yard has a lord who answers to the king. A stranger needs a plot-holder as host and deals in his yard.
laws.source: Archaeology at Sigtuna (Tesch); the first plots dated by tree rings to about 980 (?). chronicle_793.json: 975-birka-sigtuna.

laws.what: Pennies struck in the king's name at Sigtuna pass by count as well as by weight, for about thirty-five years (to about 1030).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: For once a price can be counted out. Old silver, dirhams and foreign pennies still go on the scales, and after 1030 everything does again.

laws.what: The ninth-year feast at Uppsalir, about the spring equinox, nine days long: kings and peoples, all and each, send gifts; nobody is excused. Those who have taken Christianity buy themselves off.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: If the ninth year finds you in the Svear land with a cross round your neck, it costs silver. It is also the greatest gathering of buyers in the north, with the thing and a market in the same days.
laws.source: Adam IV.27 with scholia 138-141 (?), written about 1075 from an old man's telling; Adam did not see it. The year here stands for 'from before 1000 until after 1070'; which years were ninth years is not known (?). Hkr, St Olaf's saga 76 (Laing), puts the thing and market of all Svear in late winter, moved to Candlemas after the conversion (late).

laws.what: The pact between King Olof and the heathen Svear: he may be a Christian and set up a church in the province he likes best, and must force no one from the old gods. He chose Västergötland, and a bishop sat at Skara.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: From now on Västergötland is the Christian end of the realm and Uppsalir the heathen end, with the king between. Nobody is made to choose; a merchant with a hammer and a cross on one cord gives no offence.
laws.source: Adam II.58. The year is that of the first bishop, about 1014 (?).

laws.what: Six boundary stones between the Svear king's land and the Danish king's, from the Göta river mouth to Blekinge, said to have been agreed by King Emund and a King Sven on Danaholmen.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: By the middle of the eleventh century Halland, Skåne and Blekinge are Danish, and a ship pays the Danish king at ahus. Blekinge was the Svear's in 890.
laws.source: A memorandum added to VgL (13th century); it names Sweyn Forkbeard, who was dead long before Emund, and Sawyer doubts it (?).

laws.what: Sworn merchants at Sigtuna call themselves 'the guild-brothers of the Frisians' and raise rune stones for dead brothers: one for Thorkel, one for Albod, the partner of Slode. Torbjörn cut both.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: For a Frisian this is the door to Sigtuna: guild-brothers lodge each other, witness each other's deals and bury each other. The names are Norse, so these may be Svear who trade to Frisia, or a mixed brotherhood. No guild by that name before about 1000.
laws.source: U 379 and U 391, Sigtuna, 11th century. The exact years are not known and may fall after 1066 (?).

laws.what: No traveller may be refused a roof: Adam says the Svear count it the worst shame to deny a stranger lodging, and compete for the honour of hosting him.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Lodging is not bought. It is given, and repaid with a gift and with news.

laws.what: A stranger's life is priced lower than a native's. In Västergötland: a Västgöte 21 marks, a Svea 13⅓, a Dane or Norwegian 9, a southerner or an Englishman 6. On Gotland: a Gotlander 3 marks of gold (24 of silver), any other man 10 marks of silver.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A Frisian killed in Västergötland costs his killer less than a third of a local man's price. Find a host before you find a buyer.
laws.source: VgL (about 1220) and the Guta law (about 1220), as given in Design/content/peoples/svea_gotlandic.md (?). The custom is older than the books but the sums are theirs: use lightly, for any year.

coins.what: No coin of their own and none that passes by count. Silver is weighed: rings, bars, cut pieces, and a few Frankish deniers and English pennies brought home from Dorestad. From about 800 the first Abbasid dirhams arrive by aldeigjuborg.
coins.source: The hoards and Birka's graves; Design/content/BRIEF.md rule 2 (no coinage in Scandinavia before about 825).

coins.what: Thin pennies struck at Hedeby (perhaps at Ribe too) on the pattern of Charlemagne's Dorestad deniers, with ships, stags, houses and masks. So many lay in Birka's graves that they were long called Birka coins; they were not struck there. At Birka they are silver like any other and go on the scales.
coins.source: Malmer, Nordiska mynt före år 1000 (her groups KG 3-6) (?).

coins.what: Abbasid dirhams, struck from North Africa to Central Asia, come up the rivers of Rus through the Khazars' land. On Gotland they are buried under house floors. The Spillings hoard, buried after 870/871, held 67 kg of silver in two caches (14,295 coins, nearly all dirhams, and 486 arm rings) and over 20 kg of bronze in a third. One coin is a Khazar copy on which Moses, not Muhammad, is God's messenger.
coins.source: The Spillings hoard, found 1999 at Spillings, Othem parish (Gotland Museum; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spillings_Hoard). The Moses coin is of the 830s (?).

coins.what: The weights. From about 870 traders carry folding scales in a box and two kinds of weight made to a standard tied to the dirham: small bronze cubes with cut corners, and iron balls with flat bronze-covered ends. The reckoning is the mark of 8 öre or 24 örtugar; a mark is about 200 g and an öre about 25 g (?). On Gotland silver is also worn as arm rings of even weight, so a ring is so many öre on the arm.
coins.source: Finds at Birka and on Gotland (Kyhlberg; Gustin) (?). The gram values are modern estimates (?).

coins.what: Samanid dirhams from Samarkand and Tashkent, by way of the Volga Bulghars: the flood. The peak is about 930-955. After about 965 the stream thins and the silver is worse; the last few reach the north in the 1010s.
coins.source: Coin study of the Baltic hoards (Noonan; Kovalev and Kaelin) (?). chronicle_793.json: 1000-silver-fades.

coins.what: German and English pennies take the dirham's place: Cologne pennies and the Otto-Adelheid pennies of the Harz silver (from about 990), and from 991 King Æthelred's pennies paid out as geld. All of it is cut, pecked with a knife to test it, and weighed. Gotland in all has given up over 700 hoards, more than a tonne of silver and about 168,000 coins.
coins.source: The hoards; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spillings_Hoard for the Gotland totals; rune stones U 344, U 241, U 194 for the gelds.

coins.what: The first coins of the Svear: pennies of Olof Skötkonung struck at Sigtuna by moneyers brought from England, copying Æthelred's pennies. They read OLAF REX or OLUF REX, some with SVEVORUM, and name the town as SITUN and the like; some add DEI, read as 'God's Sigtuna'. Anund Jacob's follow (ANUND REX), and a few read CNUT REX SW. About 1030 the mint stops, and no king strikes coin in the land again until the twelfth century.
coins.source: Malmer, The Sigtuna Coinage c. 995-1005 and later studies (?); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olof_Skötkonung; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anund_Jacob. chronicle_793.json: 995-sigtuna-coins.

church.what: Envoys of the Svear tell the emperor Louis that many of their people wish to take the faith. Anskar and Witmar are sent with a merchant convoy, are robbed on the way and reach Birka on foot. King Björn lets them preach for a year and a half; the prefect Herigar is baptised and builds a church on his own land. There are Christian captives in the town already.
Gautbert, a kinsman of Archbishop Ebo of Reims, is made bishop for the Svear and given the name Simon. He comes to Birka with his nephew Nithard, is well received and begins a church.
A crowd storms the bishop's house at Birka, kills Nithard, binds Gautbert and his men, plunders the house and drives them out of the land: 'not done by command of the king'.
church.source: Rimbert 17. The year is from Robinson's reckoning of the seven priestless years, 845-851 (?).

church.what: After nearly seven years with no priest, Anskar sends the hermit Ardgar to Herigar; mass is said in public again by the king's leave. Herigar dies. The rich widow Frideburg, who had kept bought wine three years for her deathbed, dies, and her daughter Catla carries her wealth to Dorestad to give to the poor there, because 'there are here but few poor'. Ardgar goes home.

Anskar comes again, 'nearly twenty days in a ship', with a token from King Horik of the Danes. A man has just told the thing that the gods are angry and offer to take the dead King Erik among them. King Olof puts the question to the lots and to two things; an old man speaks for the faith that Birka's men met at Dorestad; leave is given. Erimbert stays as priest, with a hall for prayer and a yard.
church.source: Rimbert 25-28. The year is Dreves's, followed by Robinson (?).

church.what: The priests after Erimbert: Ansfrid, a Dane, for three or four years; Ragenbert, robbed and killed on the road to Schleswig before he could sail; then Rimbert, a Dane by descent, kindly received by king and people. Anskar tells them all to ask nothing of anyone and to work with their hands. He dies in 865; no priest among the Svear is heard of for seventy years after.
church.source: Rimbert 33; Adam I.60-61 for the gap. The year stands for about 855-865 (?).

church.what: Archbishop Unni of Hamburg-Bremen sails to Birka, finds the faith forgotten, preaches, falls sick and dies there on 17 September. His body is buried at Birka; his head is taken home to Bremen.
church.source: Adam I.60-62; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Sweden for the day.

church.what: King Erik the Victorious is said to have been baptised in Denmark and to have gone back to the old gods at home.
church.source: Adam II.38 (?). The year is a guess (?).

church.what: Bruno of Querfurt writes to King Henry II that the bishop he sent over the sea to the Svear has baptised their lord, whose wife was a Christian already, with a thousand people and seven districts. Later tradition has King Olof baptised by an English bishop Sigfrid in the spring at Husaby in Västergötland.
church.source: Bruno of Querfurt's letter, 1008; the VgL king list, about 1240, for Husaby (late). Olof's pennies carry a cross from about 995, so he may have been a Christian before (?).

church.what: The see of Skara in Västergötland: Thurgot, its first bishop, is consecrated by Archbishop Unwan of Bremen. It is the only bishop's seat in the realm for nearly fifty years.
church.source: Adam II.58. The year is about 1014 (?).

church.what: From about now rune stones round the Mälar bay carry crosses and prayers for the soul; some remember men who 'died in white clothes', the robes of the newly baptised. Men and women build bridges and causeways for their kin's souls. English priests from the Norwegian king's court work in Götaland and among the Svear.
church.source: The Uppland rune stones (U 243, U 364 and others for the white clothes (?)); Adam II.57 for the English bishops.

church.what: An English priest, Wolfred, preaches to the Svear, breaks the image of Thor at the thing with an axe and is killed on the spot; his body is sunk in a marsh.
church.source: Adam II.62. The year is about 1028-1030 (?).

church.what: Gotland: Olaf Haraldsson, fleeing Norway, lies a long time in the harbour of Akergarn. Ormika of Hejnum brings him twelve rams, gets two cups and a broad axe in return, takes the faith and builds a house of prayer. Gotland's own merchants had brought priests home before: Botair of Akebäck built the first church and saw it burnt; his second, at Vi below the cliff, was spared when his father-in-law Likkair spoke for it.
church.source: GS (late). The year follows from Olaf's flight to Rus, winter 1028-1029 (?). Vi is where Visby later stands; it is not a town in the game's years.

church.what: King Emund keeps his own bishop, Osmund, consecrated in Poland and answering to no archbishop. When Bremen sends Adalvard the Elder as bishop, Osmund has him turned away at the thing; the great man Stenkil sees the envoys safe over the border. After Emund's death Adalvard sits at Skara and dies there about 1064.
church.source: Adam III.15-16; IV.23 (?). The year is between about 1055 and 1060 (?).

church.what: Under King Stenkil a bishop sits at Sigtuna: Adalvard the Younger. With Bishop Egino of Skåne he plans to burn the temple at Uppsalir; the king forbids it, saying the people would kill them and cast him out, and the bishops go to work among the Götar.
church.source: Adam IV.29-30 (?). The year is in the early 1060s (?).

church.what: After Stenkil's death and the war of the two Eriks the bishops stay away for fear. The bishop of Sigtuna goes to Skara, then home to Bremen. Halsten is driven out; Anund from Rus is cast out for refusing to sacrifice.

The temple at Uppsalir still stands and the ninth-year feast is still kept, as Adam hears it about 1075: three gods, with Thor in the middle; a grove where men and beasts are hung; Christians pay to stay away. The Svear are a people of two faiths until about 1090.
church.source: Adam IV.26-27 with scholia (?). Adam never saw it, and no temple building has been dug at Gamla Uppsala, only great halls and long rows of posts (?).

needs: A port for Sigtuna from about 980 (59.62 N, 17.72 E): ports_793.json gives the Svear no market after birka closes in 975, for the last 91 years of the game.
A realm id for the Götar ('gotar'), if any card is ever set there; they have no port on the chart.
grobin closes in 850 in ports_793.json, but chronicle_793.json burns it in 854 (854-courland-war) and Rimbert has the war in about 854: let the port run to 854.
paviken has no end year in ports_793.json; the harbour silts up and the trade moves to Västergarn beside it about 1000-1050 (?).
sources: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii, trans. C. H. Robinson, Anskar, the Apostle of the North (London 1921): https://sourcebooks.fordham.edu/basis/anskar.asp (chapters 10, 11, 14, 17, 19, 20, 25-28, 30 and 33 read tonight)
